stories.headline: France Legalises Assisted Dying After Years of Parliamentary Deadlock
stories.summary:
France's National Assembly voted 291 to 241 on Wednesday to approve a law permitting assisted dying under strict conditions, marking a landmark shift in French law after years of contentious debate. The legislation allows French adults with a serious, incurable, life-threatening illness in an advanced or terminal stage, causing unbearable and untreatable suffering, to request a lethal substance from a physician. The patient must administer the substance themselves; a doctor or nurse may assist only if the patient is physically unable to do so.

The bill had been rejected three times by France's Senate, which is dominated by right-wing parties, and had faced opposition from the Catholic Church and parts of the French medical profession. Despite the National Assembly's repeated backing, Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu announced he would refer portions of the bill to France's Constitutional Council for review before it can become law, introducing potential further delays. Opinion polls indicate a large majority of French citizens support giving terminally ill people the choice between palliative care and assisted dying.

Wednesday's vote places France alongside Belgium, the Netherlands and several other European nations that have decriminalised assisted dying in some form. Switzerland has long permitted assisted suicide provided the assisting party acts unselfishly. A similar debate is unfolding in the United Kingdom, where a bill to legalise assisted dying in England and Wales stalled earlier this year and is set to return to Parliament in September.

stories.headline: Hong Kong Police Raid Independent Bookshops, Arrest Five on National Security Grounds
stories.summary:
Hong Kong police raided two independent bookshops on Wednesday and arrested five people — two men and three women — on suspicion of violating national security legislation by displaying and selling books deemed to incite "hatred" against the territory's government, judiciary, and law enforcement agencies. Officers seized publications from both shops. If convicted, the suspects face up to seven years in prison under the territory's national security law.

One of the raided shops, Have A Nice Stay in the densely populated Mong Kok district, was founded in 2022 by former journalists and stocks literature on democracy, authoritarianism and media literacy. The raid came just one day after the bookshop announced it would close in August, citing financial pressures and what it described as an "elusive 'red line'" over which material is considered problematic by authorities. The nearby Greenfield Book Store was also reportedly targeted.

Wednesday's arrests are the third such raid on Hong Kong bookshops in 2026, following earlier arrests at the Hunter store in June and Book Punch in March. Amnesty International said the raids illustrated "the chilling reality of what the city has become," warning that uncertainty over undefined red lines has driven booksellers and writers toward self-censorship. The crackdown reflects the continued tightening of civil liberties in Hong Kong since the national security law was enacted in 2020.

stories.headline: Hegseth Orders Annual Testosterone Screenings for U.S. Troops, Offers Hormone Therapy
stories.summary:
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced Wednesday that the Department of Defense will begin annual testosterone deficiency screenings for all service members aged 30 and older, and will offer testosterone replacement therapy to those whose levels fall below optimal ranges. The program will be added to the standard periodic health assessment that troops already undergo. Hegseth framed the initiative as a means of keeping troops on the "leading edge of lethality" and ensuring service members perform at peak physical condition.

The announcement, made via a video posted to the social media platform X, has drawn both support from those who argue hormone optimization can enhance military readiness and skepticism from critics who question whether the program reflects sound medical policy or represents ideological priorities being imposed on the armed forces. The Guardian characterized the initiative as part of a broader aestheticization of military culture under Hegseth.

The Pentagon did not immediately specify the estimated cost of the program or how it would be implemented across the services. The move is the latest in a series of cultural and policy directives from Hegseth since taking office, including earlier changes to diversity and inclusion programs within the military.

stories.headline: South Africa Opens Special Probe Into Killing of Anti-Migrant Leader as Xenophobia Violence Spreads
stories.summary:
South African police have launched a special multidisciplinary investigation into the killing of Andile Mvuyelwa Somgxada, the Gauteng province leader of the anti-migrant movement March and March, who was shot outside his home east of Johannesburg earlier this month and died days later in hospital. The group's spokesperson described the killing as a targeted "hitman-type" retaliation against March and March's campaign to expel undocumented migrants from the country, and said other leaders have received death threats.

The investigation comes as South Africa's immigration crisis has escalated into widespread social unrest, with anti-migrant protesters staging weekly demonstrations and setting an unofficial June 30 deadline for undocumented foreigners to leave the country. The South African government says it has deported or repatriated more than 53,000 foreign nationals in five weeks as part of a "migration management" campaign. Separately, five people were arrested in Limpopo province for impersonating immigration officers and forcing a legally resident Nigerian national to close his business.

Acting police chief Lt. Gen. Puleng Dimpane, while announcing the special probe, issued a stern warning against vigilante enforcement, stating that no individual or group has legal authority to conduct immigration inspections or remove people from communities. March and March has publicly rejected violence, but rights groups and police say incidents of intimidation, looting, and attacks on foreign nationals have accompanied the protest movement.

Immigration has become one of the most contentious political issues in South Africa, Africa's wealthiest nation, which has long attracted economic migrants from across the continent. Analysts warn the combination of organized anti-migrant activism and the killing of a movement leader risks further inflaming tensions and increasing the potential for large-scale xenophobic violence.

stories.headline: Severe Flooding Strikes South Texas for Second Consecutive Day; Tornado Hits San Antonio
stories.summary:
Slow-moving storms continued to drench a large swath of South Texas on Wednesday, spawning a tornado in the northwestern part of San Antonio near Interstate 10 with no immediate reports of injuries. Flash flood warnings were posted across several counties near the Mexican border as forecasters warned that 10 to 20 inches of total rainfall was possible before the storm system moves out by Thursday evening.

The hardest-hit area has been Uvalde County, which recorded up to 16 inches of rain in some locations. Authorities reported at least two dozen water rescues in the city of Uvalde and activated local emergency shelters. The Texas Game Warden Search and Rescue Team and local game wardens combined to rescue at least nine people from floodwaters on Tuesday.

Texas Governor Greg Abbott issued disaster declarations for dozens of counties. Of particular concern are areas including parts of Kerr County — site of catastrophic Guadalupe River flooding last year that killed more than 100 people — where officials have been in direct contact with summer camps and retreat centers at risk of river flooding. There have been no reports of deaths or injuries from the current flooding.

Meteorologists described the pattern as a mid-summer tropical weather event that affects Texas roughly once every five years, driven by a stagnant low-pressure center drawing tropical moisture from the Gulf of Mexico and the Pacific Ocean. The storm system is expected to persist through Thursday before moving on.

stories.headline: China's Economic Growth Slows to 4.3% in Q2, Missing Beijing's Target
stories.summary:
China's economy grew at an annual rate of 4.3% in the second quarter of 2026, down sharply from 5% in the first quarter and below Beijing's target range of 4.5% to 5%, according to official GDP figures released Wednesday. It is the country's weakest quarterly expansion since late 2022, when China was still emerging from strict Covid-19 lockdowns.

Officials at China's National Bureau of Statistics cited rising external instability and an imbalance between strong supply and weak domestic demand. Separate data released alongside the GDP figures showed new home prices fell again in June, though at a slightly slower pace, while retail sales rose just 1% after contracting the previous month. Analysts note that the ongoing Iran war has driven up energy and raw materials costs, squeezing Chinese businesses that cannot pass those costs on to consumers.

Some economists caution against reading the figures as a sudden deterioration. Julian Evans-Pritchard of Capital Economics argued the slowdown may reflect Beijing's greater willingness to acknowledge pre-existing weakness following the March revision of its growth target — the lowest since 1991 — rather than a sharp new decline. June data offered some reassurance, with China's exports jumping 27% year-on-year, buoyed by surging semiconductor demand for AI infrastructure and record monthly electric vehicle exports topping one million units.

stories.headline: China Has Detained U.S. Seismologist on Espionage Charges for Nearly Two Years, Family Reveals
stories.summary:
The family of Chen Youlin, a 54-year-old American seismologist who specializes in monitoring nuclear tests, has disclosed that China detained him in November 2024 on espionage charges during a trip to Beijing to visit relatives. His family is speaking out publicly after nearly two years because they have seen no sign Beijing intends to release him. Chen is currently the only U.S. citizen formally designated as "wrongfully detained" by the U.S. government.

Chen's wife, Rong Yufang, also a seismologist, said he was interrogated more than 100 times about his work and was denied access to a lawyer for his first 13 months in custody. She described his research — which focused on using seismic data to identify North Korean nuclear tests — as transparent and collaborative with Chinese colleagues. China's foreign ministry, when asked at a Tuesday press briefing, said its judicial authorities handle cases in accordance with the law and denied any wrongful detention.

Hostage advocacy group Global Reach, which is representing the family, said there are suspicions within the U.S. government that Chen's arrest may be connected to Chinese nuclear testing activity in violation of the Comprehensive Nuclear Test Ban Treaty, and that Beijing may be seeking to learn about U.S. seismic detection methods in order to evade monitoring. Both the U.S. and China have not ratified the treaty but maintain voluntary moratoriums on explosive nuclear testing. Espionage convictions in China can carry sentences up to life imprisonment or death.

stories.headline: Venezuela's Interim Government and Opposition to Begin Formal Talks August 1
stories.summary:
Venezuela's interim government and a group of opposition politicians announced simultaneously on Tuesday that formal negotiations will begin August 1, six months after the U.S. seizure of former President Nicolás Maduro and his transfer to New York to face drug-trafficking charges. The talks were announced by both Jorge Rodríguez, who heads the government-controlled National Assembly, and an opposition group led by former lawmakers elected in 2015 — the last election widely considered free and fair.

Former Vice-President Delcy Rodríguez has governed Venezuela since Maduro's ouster with backing from the Trump administration, frustrating opposition leaders who had hoped his removal would lead to a change in government. Jorge Rodríguez cited the twin earthquakes that struck northern Venezuela on June 24 — killing at least 4,734 confirmed dead with the toll still rising — as a catalyst for dialogue, saying "only through unity can we move forward with reconstruction." The opposition's statement described the talks as laying down "a route map towards democracy" and credited U.S. support in the earthquake aftermath as evidence that "Venezuela is not alone."

The opposition team will be led by Dinorah Figuera, who returned from nearly eight years in exile in June at the invitation of the U.S. State Department. Talks will prioritize strengthening democratic institutions, reforming the National Electoral Council — which declared Maduro the winner of the disputed 2024 presidential election despite evidence showing opposition candidate Edmundo González won overwhelmingly — and providing guarantees for political participation.

stories.headline: Italy's Meloni Suffers Surprise Parliamentary Defeat on Electoral Reform Amendment
stories.summary:
Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni suffered a significant setback Wednesday when her coalition government lost a key vote on an electoral reform amendment in the lower house of parliament by a margin of 188 to 187. The secret ballot result, which rejected a provision on preference voting that would allow voters to select preferred candidates from party lists, indicated that several members of Meloni's own Brothers of Italy party voted against the government.

The broader electoral reform package, which would move Italy to a fully proportional voting system with a bonus for the largest party or coalition, can still proceed without the defeated amendment. Meloni described the outcome as "a missed opportunity for Italians" and did not address opposition calls to resign and hold early elections ahead of the vote currently scheduled for autumn 2027. Opposition parties, which have been uniting ahead of next year's contest, celebrated in parliament.

Critics had characterized the reform as "authoritarian" and an attempt to secure a stronger majority in the next election, while Meloni argued it would produce more stable governing coalitions. The defeat follows an earlier blow to her government this spring, when a government-backed constitutional reform referendum failed after opposition parties campaigned jointly against it. Tensions within her coalition have been rising as the constituent parties' individual poll numbers have declined.

stories.headline: Update: Iran Strikes U.S. Allies in Kuwait, Bahrain, Jordan as Trump Threatens Civilian Infrastructure
stories.summary:
The U.S.-Iran conflict entered a fourth consecutive day of direct exchanges on Wednesday, with Iran claiming to have struck U.S. military assets in Kuwait, Bahrain, Jordan, and Oman hours after a new wave of American air strikes hit Iranian targets. The U.S. military confirmed it launched fresh strikes against Iran at 6 a.m. ET Wednesday, targeting ballistic missile infrastructure, nuclear sites, and naval bases. President Trump simultaneously reinstated a naval blockade on Iranian ports and announced a 20% charge on cargo transiting the Strait of Hormuz.

Trump escalated his rhetoric Wednesday, warning that the U.S. would bomb Iranian civilian infrastructure if no deal is reached within a week. He called the memorandum of understanding signed roughly a month ago a "dead letter." Iran declared the Strait of Hormuz closed and launched broad attacks on U.S. allies and bases throughout the region, with the Iran-backed Houthis separately striking Abha airport in Saudi Arabia.

The confrontation, now more than four months old, shows no clear diplomatic off-ramp. Senate Democrats blocked the annual National Defense Authorization Act this week over what they called an unauthorized war, with Minority Leader Chuck Schumer calling the defense bill a "permission slip for recklessness." Republican supporters of the administration argue sustained military pressure is necessary to prevent Iran from threatening Israel and regional stability.

The conflict is reshaping global energy markets and testing U.S. alliances across the Middle East. Trump said he had spoken with regional leaders — described as "kings and emirs" — who proposed alternative arrangements to the Hormuz toll, though specifics were not disclosed. The situation remains fluid, with military analysts warning that any attempt to seize or hold Iranian territory such as Kharg Island would carry severe risks from missile and drone counterattacks.

stories.headline: Ebola Outbreak in Congo Surpasses 2,000 Cases and 750 Deaths as WHO Loses Track of Transmission Chains
stories.summary:
Confirmed Ebola cases in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo have reached 2,011, with 754 confirmed deaths, according to government data released Wednesday. Health authorities describe it as the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak on record, with the World Health Organization warning that 80 percent of new cases are emerging from unknown chains of transmission — a critical indicator that the outbreak is spreading faster than contact tracers can track.

The loss of visibility into transmission chains severely hampers containment efforts, as responders cannot identify and isolate those who may have been exposed. The affected region in eastern Congo faces compounding challenges including ongoing armed conflict, displacement, and limited healthcare infrastructure, all of which obstruct outbreak response operations.

Funding cuts to global health programs have further constrained the international response, according to public health officials. The WHO and partner organizations are working to scale up case detection, vaccination, and community engagement, but the sheer pace of spread is outrunning those efforts.

Ebola virus disease carries a high fatality rate and spreads through direct contact with the bodily fluids of infected individuals. Previous outbreaks have been contained through aggressive contact tracing, isolation, and ring vaccination — methods that depend on knowing who has been exposed, a prerequisite that the current outbreak is rapidly eroding.

stories.headline: Todd Blanche and Jay Clayton Face Senate Confirmation Hearings for Attorney General and Intelligence Director
stories.summary:
Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche appeared before the Senate Judiciary Committee Wednesday for his confirmation hearing to be permanently confirmed as the nation's top law enforcement officer. Blanche, who previously served as President Trump's personal defense attorney in the hush-money case, faces scrutiny over his role in high-profile DOJ decisions including investigations, indictments, the rollout of Epstein files, and a since-scrapped $1.776 billion "anti-weaponization" fund that triggered a Republican revolt last month.

Separately, Jay Clayton, the U.S. attorney for the Southern District of New York, appeared before the Senate Intelligence Committee for his confirmation hearing to become director of national intelligence, succeeding acting DNI Bill Pulte. Democrats have raised concerns that the Trump administration could use intelligence agencies to interfere with midterm elections. Clayton's nomination came after Trump derailed an earlier confirmation process on social media.

Blanche will need the votes of all Judiciary Committee Republicans to advance, making the hearing a high-stakes test at a moment when the Senate's Republican coalition is navigating its first major nomination battle without the late Sen. Lindsey Graham. Democrats, led by Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, have announced opposition to Blanche. Supporters, including more than 670,000 sworn law enforcement officers and 300 angel families, have expressed backing for his confirmation.

The dual hearings represent one of the most consequential confirmation days of Trump's second term, placing the leadership of both the Justice Department and the intelligence community under Senate scrutiny simultaneously. Republicans frame both nominees as experienced professionals suited to their roles; Democrats argue Blanche's deep personal and professional ties to Trump make him unfit to serve as an independent law enforcement officer.

stories.headline: House Passes Sunshine Protection Act to Make Daylight Saving Time Permanent
stories.summary:
The U.S. House of Representatives voted 308-117 on Tuesday to approve the Sunshine Protection Act, a bipartisan bill that would eliminate the twice-yearly clock change and make daylight saving time permanent across the country. The legislation now heads to the Senate, where an identical bill introduced by Florida Republican Rick Scott awaits action.

President Trump has publicly backed the measure, writing in May that he would "work very hard" to see the change enacted and calling the current system a "ridiculous, twice yearly production." The bill drew votes from both parties, reflecting years of bipartisan frustration with the current system, which dates to World War One-era energy conservation policies and was standardized nationally in 1966.

Critics of permanent daylight saving time argue it would produce dangerously dark winter mornings, worsening road conditions for early commuters. Health researchers who favor permanent standard time contend that morning light exposure supports better sleep cycles and overall well-being. Hawaii, Arizona, and several U.S. territories have already opted out of clock changes entirely.

The Senate's path for the bill remains uncertain, with previous versions of similar legislation stalling in that chamber despite House passage. If enacted, the change would affect hundreds of millions of Americans and align the U.S. with a global trend away from seasonal time shifts.
